name: Polybutylene Adipate Terephthalate (PBAT): Against Pollution
notation_note: A random copolyester. The flexible aliphatic adipate segments are what bacteria can attack; the rigid aromatic terephthalate segments are what make it strong enough to use.
historical_events_referenced: United Nations Earth Summit, Rio de Janeiro, June 1992

historical_images.alt: An aerial photograph of Sugarloaf Mountain in Rio de Janeiro, with a cable car passing in the foreground and a large white banner reading 'SOLD / VENDIDO' with a Greenpeace logo hung across the rock face.
historical_images.caption: A Greenpeace banner on Sugarloaf Mountain during the June 1992 Earth Summit, protesting what activists saw as a conference trading firm commitments for compromise.
historical_images.author: Celso Meira

historical_images.alt: A wide view across farmland toward a large chemical plant on the horizon, its skyline dense with distillation towers, storage tanks and a tall red-and-white striped chimney.
historical_images.caption: Part of BASF's Ludwigshafen site, where PBAT was developed through the early 1990s and first sold, as ecoflex, in 1998.
historical_images.author: Felix König

historical_images.alt: A folded compostable plastic bag printed with green leaf logos and multilingual 'bio and compostable' text, laid beside a wrapped set of disposable cutlery marked with the same certification symbols and the brand name Mater-Bi.
historical_images.caption: Compostable bags and cutlery made with Mater-Bi, Novamont's brand for starch blended with an aliphatic-aromatic copolyester in the same family as PBAT.
historical_images.author: JKey128

historical_images.alt: Two long windrows of dark, decomposing organic material piled beside a paved yard, with an open-sided barn and trees in the background.
historical_images.caption: A central composting site in Germany, the kind of industrial-scale facility where a certified compostable film has to prove it breaks down on schedule.
historical_images.author: Crystalclear

synthesis.industrial_process_notes: Developed to address environmental concerns about PET plastic persistence -- roughly 30% of global PET production becomes bottles, of which only 15-35% is recycled. Major manufacturers: BASF (ecoflex), Novamont (Origo-Bi), Eastman Chemical (Eastar Bio), and numerous Chinese suppliers.

crystallinity_typical.conditions: Random copolymer structure prevents significant crystallization, giving a wide melting range rather than a sharp Tm.

structure_morphology.chain_flexibility_notes: Low elastic modulus and stiffness, but high flexibility and toughness -- properties comparable to LDPE, which is what makes it a practical drop-in replacement for LDPE film in compostable applications.

tm.conditions: Random copolymer gives a wide melting range rather than a single sharp value; no specific range sourced.

tensile_modulus.conditions: Qualitatively 'low elastic modulus'; no specific number sourced.

hydrolysis_resistance.value: Fully biodegradable when composted; ~90% degradation after 80 days (BASF ecoflex test)

environmental.degradation_pathway: Butylene adipate groups enable biodegradation under composting conditions (~90% degradation after 80 days per BASF ecoflex testing).
environmental.environmental_notes: Does not degrade in marine and fresh water -- an important caveat similar to PLA's marine-litter limitation.
